items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: Red Rodney who had been close to Bird

ctx.x: Before we get to ABC Paramount I want to kind of talk about something that I think was very pivotal because I think we are near the year 1955. What did the death of Charlie Parker do to kind of change the whole scene and how did it affect you personally?

It wasn’t apparent that his death was going to have the impact that it did. I mean obviously you miss someone who is important to everybody’s developed, who is the major figure, only musician with the nightclub named after him and all that sort of stuff. Charlie Parker, his passing left… gave more of a feeling of urgency to defining what his music was about and what… because there was a big conflict between bebop and cool. And right around that time, Stan Kentin was coming forth and Dave Bluebeck was

coming forth with what was called progressive jazz. So there was a lot of confusion in what was being printed about the music. So those of us who were looking at the family lineage of jazz were thinking we really have to cautify this music and put it into perspective for ourselves you know before you know we can put it into perspective for anybody else. Art [Unintelligible] and a lot of people were very, very conscious of this. Dizzy felt the loss perhaps more than anyone, having been that close to Charlie and…
